source.title: Specialization after Generalization: Towards Understanding Test-Time Training in Foundation Models
source.authors: Jonas Hübotter; Patrik Wolf; A. Shevchenko; Dennis Jüni; Andreas Krause; Gil Kur

record.tranche_reason: The study scales Qwen2.5 model size and reports Pile test-set bits per byte, a different experimental setup from the original scaling-law studies. It does not fit or test a power-law curve.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work as background. Its relevant result is a model-size sweep of language-model test loss; it does not test token or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or extrapolation from fitted laws.
record.test_reason: The study cites scaling laws as motivation for calling foundation models underparameterized. Its language result is the gap between test-time training (TTT) and the untouched Qwen2.5 base models (0.5B–32B) in Pile bits per byte, read from Figure 4. The base-model curve is only a baseline. Its values are not given numerically, and the study does not fit or assess a power law, extrapolate, vary tokens or compute, or examine allocation or shape. The models are an off-the-shelf family, not a controlled sweep. The MNIST and ImageNet sweeps measure classification error of small CNN and MLP heads with no power-law analysis. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that TTT gives the largest gains for underparameterized models and that these gains shrink with model size. They draw no conclusion on the form of loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates Qwen2.5 base models on Pile test bits per byte as part of a TTT scaling experiment; it does not use the original studies' fitting and extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: For the language-model experiment, TTT uses 50 neighbors, one gradient step per neighbor, and LoRA; only 1% of parameters are fine-tuned.

fits_no_version.finding: TTT on nearest neighbours lowers Pile bits per byte, MNIST error and ImageNet error relative to global training. The gain shrinks as model size grows (Figure 4, Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of test-time training over a globally trained model diminishes with model scale.

record.problems: The language-model results are shown in a figure without exact per-model bits-per-byte values in the text. The study does not fit or test a power law, and does not sweep training tokens or compute.

untested.parts: No power-law fit, no token or compute sweep, and the base-model loss values are not reported numerically. The sweep spans under two orders of magnitude in parameters.
The MNIST and ImageNet size and data sweeps report error rates with no power-law form assessed.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' for V1 is not supported. A figure of off-the-shelf model losses used as a baseline, with no fit or analysis of the scaling form, does not bear on whether loss follows a power law.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports Pile test bits per byte across Qwen2.5 sizes, but does not fit or assess a power-law form, test several orders of magnitude, or vary training tokens or compute.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 0.5B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated language-model test loss in the model-size sweep.
rows.measure: Bits per byte on the Pile test set
rows.uncertainty: 90% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping with 1000 samples
rows.note: The plotted value is not numerically stated in the text. The paper describes this as language modeling performance and says TTT's performance gap shrinks with model size; it does not state a fitted loss law.
rows.check: This is the global-training baseline in a TTT comparison, not a test of power-law loss scaling. The value is figure-only and no law is fitted.
